Gastroenterology · published research

Anal fistula

Summary of the Evidence

Two relevant publications were identified: one small nonrandomized controlled study of mixed postoperative anorectal wounds and one rat experiment on fistula-in-ano. The clinical study included patients after surgery for fistula, abscess, or hemorrhoids and did not report fistula-specific healing outcomes. The animal study directly evaluated a surgically created fistula tract (Nurfitri et al. 2025; Dos Santos et al. 2021).

Human and clinical evidence

The clinical study enrolled 10 participants and compared near-infrared PBM plus routine care with routine care alone over five days. Wound width decreased more in the PBM group, whereas the difference in wound-length reduction was small. Because results were pooled across several anorectal procedures, the study does not establish fistula-tract closure, recurrence prevention, or a patient-important benefit specific to anal fistula (Nurfitri et al. 2025).

Animal evidence

In a rat fistula model, 660-nm laser treatment reduced the mean residual tract area compared with control and was associated with lower inflammatory-infiltrate and vascular-congestion scores. No animal in either group achieved complete tract closure. The findings support a local tissue-response signal but not definitive fistula healing (Dos Santos et al. 2021).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The human study used an 808-nm near-infrared laser at 100 mW/cm² for 900 seconds per session, delivered on days 0, 1, 2, 3, and 5. The rat study used a 660-nm laser at three points along the tract on each treatment day for 30 days. The clinical evidence is indirect because it combines different postoperative wounds, while the animal model cannot establish effectiveness in human fistula care.

Interpretation

The evidence suggests that PBM may accelerate one short-term wound-dimension measure after mixed anorectal surgery and may reduce tract area and inflammation in rats. It does not demonstrate fistula closure or reduced recurrence. Certainty is low for short-term wound-width change and very low for fistula-specific healing outcomes.

Publications and records

2 relevant publications

Clinical effect sizes (estimate)

Mixed postoperative anorectal wounds at day 5. Wound width decreased 46% with PBM and 26% in controls; wound length decreased 35% with PBM and 30% in controls. The publication combined fistula, abscess, and hemorrhoid surgery, so no fistula-specific effect estimate is available (Nurfitri et al. 2025).

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low for short-term wound-width change in mixed postoperative anorectal wounds.

Very low for fistula-tract closure or recurrence prevention.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

One small nonrandomized study combined several postoperative anorectal wounds and followed dimensions for five days, so its favorable width result is indirect for anal fistula and does not address tract closure or recurrence. One rat experiment reduced tract area and inflammation but achieved no complete closures. These limitations support low certainty for short-term wound dimensions and very low certainty for fistula healing.
